title: Register, grant, call: the agent gets its own identity
takeaway: One key is the agent's whole identity: scopes, custodian, caps and expiry hang off it. The grant is what lets it reach one tool.

steps.say: {{custodian}} registers {{agent_label}} as {{agent}}: scope mcp, custodian {{custodian}}, one year expiry. The registry mints the VirtualKey; nobody chooses it.
The key is granted to {{app}}, tool {{tool}} only. The grant names the key, not its value.
{{agent_label}} calls {{tool}} on {{app}} with its key.

title: Revoke the agent and the gateway refuses it
takeaway: Revoke is the only non-destructive kill. The key, its caps and its grants stay; the gateway answers 401 and does not say why.

steps.say: {{agent_label}} is registered as {{agent}}.
Granted to {{app}}.
It works.
{{custodian}} retires the agent: Revoked:true. Nothing is deleted.
The same call now gets 401. A revoked key looks exactly like an unknown one on the wire; only the gateway log says which.

title: Scope too narrow, and an app that was never granted
takeaway: Two different 403s. A missing scope names itself; a missing grant is a bare 403 that only the gateway log explains.

steps.say: {{agent_label}} is registered with the mcp scope only.
Granted to {{app}} and nothing else.
It tries an agent-to-agent call. The key has no a2a scope: the one self-describing refusal.

expect.bodyIncludes: key not scoped for a2a access

steps.say: It tries {{other_app}}, which it was never granted. Bare 403 Forbidden, no reason on the wire.

title: Per-key rate cap: the 429 shape
takeaway: Caps are registration attributes on the key. Over the cap the gateway answers 429 with retry-after; waiting clears it. Enforcement policy belongs to the kill-switch demo, not this one.

steps.say: {{agent_label}} is registered for llm with RPMLimit 3. An llm key needs the upstream RealKey at create time.
Call 1.
Call 2.
Call 3.
Call 4 in the same minute: 429 tokens_rate_limit_exceeded with a retry-after header.
The virtual clock moves 61 seconds. Nothing sleeps.
The window has passed; the call succeeds again.

title: In-place rotation does not exist; replacement does
takeaway: A PUT with a new VirtualKey returns 200 and changes nothing. Real rotation is snapshot, create successor, verify, revoke the old.

steps.say: {{agent_label}} is registered with a guardrail set to block and a 60/min cap.
Granted to {{app}}.
UNSAFE: someone PUTs a new VirtualKey hoping to rotate. The registry returns 200. The value is ignored.
The old key still works, because nothing rotated.
SAFE: snapshot the spec, create {{agent_next}} from it, copy its grants, verify it with a real call, then revoke the old key.
The old value now gets 401: the leak window is closed.
The successor works, with a new VirtualKey, and carries the same caps and guardrail.

title: Deleting an llm key without its RealKey is a one-way door
takeaway: Reads return RealKey as an empty string, so a deleted llm key cannot be recreated unless you hold the upstream key. Revoke instead.

steps.say: {{agent_label}} is registered for llm, with a RealKey.
A read shows RealKey as an empty string. The registry will never hand it back.
Someone tries to delete it to rotate. THIS DEMO refuses (the real API would let you): recreate would need the RealKey nobody can read back.
Revoke instead: the agent is dead to the gateway and nothing is lost.
Calls are refused.

title: Delete and recreate under the same name: grants come back
takeaway: Grants reference keys by name. A new key with the old name silently inherits the old key's access, including access nobody reviewed for the new key.

steps.say: {{agent}} is registered with mcp scope and granted to {{app}}.
Granted to {{app}}.
The key is deleted (no llm scope, so nothing is lost). The grant is not removed.
The registry now holds a dangling grant that names a key that does not exist.

steps.name: {{agent}}
steps.say: Someone creates a NEW key with the same name, a different custodian, and never grants it anything.
The new key reaches {{app}}: it inherited the grant by name.
The warning list flags the grant as inherited. In the real product nothing flags it.

title: Workload identity: an agent with no static secret
takeaway: The key trusts an external issuer instead of holding a secret. The audience is mandatory and the token lifetime is capped. Gateway acceptance on the real product is UNVERIFIED.

steps.say: {{agent_label}} is registered as a workload identity: issuer {{issuer}}, audience {{audience}}, one subject, 5 minute lifetime cap. No VirtualKey is minted.
Granted to {{app}} like any other key.
The workload presents the issuer's token (mock claims; signatures are not simulated). The gateway accepts it.
A token minted for a different audience is refused: an unbound token would be replayable elsewhere.
A token that lives an hour exceeds the 5 minute cap and is refused.

title: Expiry retires an agent on its own, and editing renews it
takeaway: An expired key is refused like an unknown one. Moving NotAfter forward renews it, so put every expiry on a calendar.

steps.say: {{agent_label}} is registered with a one hour expiry.
Granted to {{app}}.
Inside the hour it works.
Two hours pass on the virtual clock.
The key has expired: 401, same shape as an unknown key.
{{custodian}} edits the key and moves NotAfter forward. Editing an expired key is renewing it.
Same VirtualKey, working again.
